blocks.text: Appendix Two: Buddha and Mara Are of One Mind

inline.s: The good and evil of human beings all arise from the mind. When the mind is good, one is a Buddha; when the mind is evil, one is a Mara. Buddha and Mara originally have no fixed nature; they simply shift according to the good or evil of one’s thoughts. Honesty, humility, compassion, and diligence are good thoughts; deceit, arrogance, hatred, and lustful indolence are evil thoughts. Thus when a single thought of goodness arises, the Buddha responds, and body, mind, and environment become harmonious and serene, so that one is transformed toward the Buddha. Not only does the good become ever better, but the wicked are also turned toward the good. When a single thought of evil arises, Mara responds, and body, mind, and environment turn harsh and base, so that one is transformed toward Mara. Not only does the wicked become ever worse, but the good are also turned toward the evil. Hence the saying, “Common beings and sages are within a single mind; good and evil are both wrought by the mind.” When the mind is Buddha, one is Buddha; when the mind is Mara, one is Mara; such is the inherent principle. In the age of the Latter Dharma most people are deluded and benighted, unable to tell good from evil, and so bring suffering upon themselves. Still worse are those who harbor crooked hearts while putting on fair words, thinking that all others can be deceived and that none in the world is as clever as they. Little do they know that baleful demons and evil spirits are already gathering upon their body and mind; once their karma is set in motion, at the least it brings illness, bereavement, and calamity, at the worst sinking them into the evil destinies. Even if past wholesome causes spare them for a while, once their merit is exhausted, retribution without end follows — how perilous! Such is the way in which doing good brings blessings and doing evil brings misfortune, and it has held true through the ages without ever failing. In short, Buddha and Mara never depart from one’s own mind. Why? Because everything is created by the mind alone. As the saying goes, when the mind arises all dharmas arise, and when the mind ceases all dharmas cease. Yet dharmas have no self-nature and are neither crooked nor upright: when the mind is right, even practicing a wrong dharma makes that dharma right; when the mind is wrong, even practicing the right dharma makes that dharma wrong. When the mind is good, Mara is turned into Buddha; when the mind is evil, Buddha is turned into Mara. In the very moment we set a thought in motion, how could we fail to be on our guard?!

blocks.text: Appendix Three: A Record of Master Huiming

inline.s: I recall that in the summer of the thirteenth year of the Republic I left the Wuchang Institute of Buddhist Studies for the second time and went to Guanghua Temple on Solitary Hill by West Lake in Hangzhou to found the monthly journal “Lion’s Roar” in order to promote a reform of Buddhism. I was betrayed by the abbot Zhenhao and suffered the combined blows of the local criminal element and the hostile forces about it, so the journal “Lion” was stillborn and I was unjustly held behind iron bars for more than ten days. Disheartened and weary, I took up quarters at Lingyin Temple in the recitation hall, gathering my mind and cultivating stillness, and in this way I was able to draw near to the eminent monk of his generation, the Elder Master Huiming. It happened that Katsuo-dera in Osaka, Japan, had opened an “Esoteric Buddhist Academy” and, under the banner of repaying the kindness of its source, was recruiting students from Chinese Buddhism free of charge. With the help of the Elder Master Huiming, toward the end of that year I invited the fellow residents, the two masters Tan Xuan of Hunan and Xiao Wu of Henan, to go there together to study.

To speak of the Elder Master Huiming, abbot of Hangzhou’s Lingyin Temple, there was no one from one end of the land to the other who did not know him, and he was especially praised by all the home-leaving Ch’an monks of every quarter. He was a native of Fujian and, I am told, left home in his youth. When I came to know him he was already an old man nearing seventy, short and slight, only a little over five feet tall, with bronze-colored skin, a striking head and high cheekbones, and a voice that boomed like a great bell. When he preached the Dharma in the main hall his voice set the temple’s bronze bell to humming, a sign of how extraordinary a man he was. To look at him, he resembled precisely the arhat who tames the dragon and subdues the tiger in the Arhat Hall, much like the bodily image of the Sixth Patriarch enshrined in the Patriarch Hall of Nanhua Temple in Guangdong.

The Elder Master Huiming had been a farmer in lay life and had never learned to read; after leaving home, all his labors were a life of ascetic practice. In the monastery he served in the outer offices, holding the hard-worn posts of vegetable cook, rice cook, water keeper, and cleaner, and in his spare time he delighted in sitting cross-legged and pondering Ch’an. How did this illiterate, toiling monk come to bear the honorific of a Dharma master? It is in truth something of a marvel. According to what the old-timers of the forests tell, when Master Huiming served as a server in the dining hall of Tiantong Temple in Ningbo — the duty of filling the bowls of the assembled community — he fed the dogs after every meal, and this counted as one of his daily routine tasks. He could not bear to throw away the rice the dogs had left; to cherish his blessings he would take it up, rinse it in water, and eat it himself. He did this for several years. One day, as he ate the rice the dogs had left, he suddenly burst into loud laughter. His fellow monks asked what he was laughing at. He said, “I have often heard people say that a dog has Buddha-nature. Today I understood this principle, and that is why I laugh.” From that time on it seems he had awakened into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. This is exactly what is meant by “the lowest of persons may hold the highest wisdom.”

After that, Tiantong Temple invited a master to lecture on the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment. Although he was of the menial staff, he was most zealous, following the assembly every day to hear the sutra. One day he heard the master expound the passage, “The nature of perfect enlightenment is not a nature; in its nature it yet exists; it rises along with all natures, without grasping and without attaining,” and at once his mind opened and his understanding cleared, so that he suddenly beheld his own nature. After every lecture he would even set forth the meaning to his fellow monks, showing his grasp of the scripture. His fellow monks all mocked him, saying, “Look at your face in a mirror. With such a hard-bitten look and not a single character to your name, do you still fancy yourself a lecturer of the sutras?” Unable to contain his indignation, he answered, “Do you take me for one who cannot become a Dharma master? Very well, from today I am determined to become one just to show you, and in three years I shall return to Tiantong to lecture on the sutras! Just you wait and see!” When his fellow monks heard such big talk they all clapped their hands and laughed outright. Some said, “If a fellow of your stamp could become a lecturing Dharma master, then only when an iron tree puts forth blossoms and the waters of the Yellow River flow backward.” He said nothing further in dispute, but went straight back to his room, gathered up his robe and bedding, shouldered his bundle, and walked out of the monastery gate.

After leaving Tiantong he wandered about on foot everywhere, emulating Sudhana’s fifty-three visits, seeking out good teachers in every quarter, and making pilgrimages to the four great sacred mountains of China; before he knew it three years had passed. In the spring of the third year he heard that Tiantong Temple was again holding a sutra-lecture assembly, expounding the Sutra of the Great Vaipulya Buddha’s Adornment. The thought stirred in him, and he shouldered his bundle and came back to Tiantong. When he entered the guest hall and sat down, the guest master, seeing that he had only a shabby bundle, that he was short and small, and that he bore a hard-bitten look, took him for an ordinary wandering cloud-and-water monk. Putting on a stern face, he asked, “Master, what business have you at this monastery?” He answered, “I have come to hear the sutras and to beg an auditor’s seat of the temple.” The guest master thought to himself in amusement, “A toiler like you, and attend sutra lectures?” and so he teased him, “Do you know what sutra is being lectured on here?” He lifted his head and replied, “Why ever need you ask? Is it not the Sutra of the Great Vaipulya Buddha’s Adornment?” The guest master jested further, “And do you know how the three words “great, vaipulya, adornment” are to be explained? Tell me; if you explain them aright, I shall grant you the seat.” Seeing that the guest master was deliberately putting him to the proof, he dropped his smile and, pointing at him, said, “How little you have studied! How can you ask about the Dharma with a flippant mind? If you would seek instruction from me, you must be reverent and respectful: don your robe, spread your sitting mat, prostrate yourself to me three times, and then kneel before me with palms joined; only then will I explain it to you. Is such a child’s-play attitude the way to seek the Dharma?” Smarting under this rebuke, the guest master felt that although the man’s appearance was unremarkable, he was by no means ordinary, and so he quickly made an apologetic bow, saying, “Very well, pray sit a moment; I shall be right back.”

That guest master turned and hurried to the abbot’s quarters, where he played upon the abbot a trick of “veiled deception,” saying that an unusual monk had just come to lodge there, that he declared himself come to hear the sutras and to beg an auditor’s seat, that when asked what sutra he wished to hear he had answered, the Sutra of the Great Vaipulya Buddha’s Adornment, and that when the guest master asked how the three words “great, vaipulya, adornment” were explained, the monk’s tone was anything but humble, saying that the meaning of those three words could only be explained if the abbot himself donned his robe, took up his sitting mat, and invited him to the abbot’s quarters. When the abbot heard the guest master’s account, his curiosity was stirred, and he truly wrapped himself in his great crimson robe, took up his mat, and came to the guest hall, where he invited the monk Huiming to the abbot’s quarters. Once inside, the monk Huiming said to the abbot, “Venerable, if you would hear my words on the Dharma, you must lend me your Dharma seat.” The abbot agreed and respectfully installed him upon the seat. Seated there, he looked the very image of a Dharma master. He struck the block and began, “Venerable, the three words “great, vaipulya, adornment” each admit four lines of explanation: within broad there is broad, within broad there is measure, within measure there is broad, and within measure there is measure. If I speak of the meaning of broad-within-broad, a whole lifetime would not see it done. To use the two lines of broad-within-measure and measure-within-broad would pass a year or half a year. But if I take up the line of measure-within-measure, I may discourse a while with you. I wonder which line the Venerable would care to hear?” Hearing this, the abbot realized this wandering monk was no simple person and dared not treat him lightly; he answered, “Pray, speak of measure-within-measure.” Thereupon he gave forth a great lion’s roar. What was meant by “great,” what by “square,” what by “broad” — he discoursed upon the threefold profound meaning of essence, character, and function of these three words, speaking freely from his own nature, like one whose bucket bottom had fallen out, pouring forth for a full three hours. The abbot, the more he listened, the more delighted he grew, feeling that every principle set forth flowed from the monk’s own self-nature, fell into no old ruts of the ancients, and was marked by original insight — inexhaustibly subtle and captivating. Straightway he prostrated himself in homage and, exclaiming again and again, “How excellent, Master! How excellent, Master!” begged him to lecture in his stead. This was the origin of the title of Dharma master by which the monk Huiming came to be honored, and the very first time he ever lectured on the sutras.

From that time on, monasteries in every quarter, admiring the fame of Master Huiming, vied to invite him to lecture, and at every lecture the seats were never empty. Though he had gained the name of a lecturing Dharma master, he did not labor over words and books; his interest lay in meditation. His lectures were delivered entirely from his own understanding, unlike other lecturing masters who relied on commentaries. He held that the principles in the commentaries were the views of earlier men and had nothing to do with himself; to recite the commentaries from memory was but to count another man’s treasure. So in lecturing he never classified doctrines, but only clarified the text and explained the meaning, delighting in the inspirational kung-ans and stories — and for this he was gladly heard by Ch’an monks and laymen and laywomen alike. As soon as word went out that Master Huiming was to lecture somewhere, the Ch’an monks and lay followers would stream after him, a sight never seen with ordinary lecturing masters. Though the Elder was a man who knew not a single character, the Dharma words he spoke were most refined. That year I spent the New Year at Lingyin; on New Year’s Eve he ascended the hall and spoke, and I recall two lines of his teaching: “Blossom by blossom the flowers bloom fair; petal by petal the plum leaves its fragrance.” How full of poetry! Could such words come from one who had never touched ink? Clearly they were the fruit of his enlightenment. (There is a volume of the Recorded Sayings of Master Huiming, set down by Master Tan Xuan of Hunan.)

In the half year I spent in the presence of the Elder Master Huiming, I felt this great worthy had many singular ways about him. The first was his distaste for vanity, and one fact proves it. In the 1920s, when Hangzhou’s Lingyin Temple was made an open ten-direction monastery (it had been a temple of a hereditary lineage), the elders of the surrounding monasteries and the supporting lay Buddhists of Hangzhou gathered to choose a first abbot. Esteeming Master Huiming’s deep attainment and weighty virtue, they all recommended the Elder as abbot of Lingyin, but he declined; though they pleaded with him again and again, he would not consent. After half a year they hit upon a stratagem: several noted local laymen came forward to invite the Elder to Lingyin Temple for a vegetarian meal, and suspecting no design, he accepted and went. The moment he stepped inside Lingyin’s mountain gate he saw monks standing in rows on both sides, all robed and holding their sitting mats, as if awaiting a great guest. Perceiving that things were amiss, he knew he had been tricked! At once he wheeled about and took to his heels. They gave chase, barred his way, and begged him to return. He thereupon sat himself on the ground, crossed his legs, and refused to rise at any cost. There was no helping it, so they lifted him and carried him back, bearing him into the Hall of the Heavenly Kings while the bells and drums sounded together and firecrackers were set off. He wept and cried out loudly; and even when they bore him to the abbot’s quarters and placed him upon the Dharma seat he would not stop wailing. The whole company knelt and cried in unison, “We congratulate the Venerable!” Weeping still, he said, “I am no material for an abbot. That you should all hold me so dear has in truth undone me. I have neither the Way, nor virtue, nor any practice whatever — what capacity have I to lead the assembly? Better choose some worthy one; I beg you all, in your compassion, to let me go!” And with that he fell to weeping again. Only when they all kneeled and pleaded, declaring they would not rise unless he consented, did the Elder reluctantly agree to stand in as abbot of Lingyin.

Although the Elder Master Huiming served as abbot of Hangzhou’s foremost monastery, a position and title so exalted, his whole manner of life yet remained as of old — still the bearing of a Ch’an monk. Every day he ate his meals in the hall with the community, partaking of no private dishes and sharing the very same grains of rice. In his bedroom there was nothing but a wooden frame bed; a single table stood in the room, and upon it was no ornament at all — only a teapot and a teacup. On the bed were only one worn cotton quilt, two tattered patched robes, and a set of old, worn spare underclothes. Even when devotees offered him new clothes, within a couple of days he would have turned them over to others. The band of rogue arhats of Hangzhou who had no clothes to wear and no money to spend would all come running to Lingyin to sponge off the Elder; and to these rogue arhats the Elder was most sympathetic, refusing none who came, answering every request, giving whatever was asked, never stinting.

The Elder Master Huiming was so full of compassion, loving-kindness, joy, and giving, and precisely because of this he got into no end of comical scrapes. He would go out and often come home transformed: either his great-sleeved outer robe was gone and he returned in only his short shirt and trousers, or his underclothes had been stripped off by the rogue arhats and he came back stark bare, wearing only the empty shell of his robe, pinching the hem between two fingers and walking home with an abashed look. Once the joke was worse still. The Elder, having gone early in the morning to a devotee’s house for an alms meal, was returning past the Broken Bridge at West Lake when he met a crowd of rogue arhats. The instant they saw him they pressed in all together, one begging for his outer robe, one for his jacket, one for his trousers. Smiling, the Elder satisfied them all, pulling off one garment after another and giving them over, until he was stripped wholly bare! He could not face anyone; it was most mortifying! Having no help for it, he jumped into the lake, sank his body beneath the water, and kept only his head above the surface, and so he soaked there until the sun was down behind the western hills, meaning to wait for darkness and slip away. Just then he caught sight of an acquaintance crossing the bridge, and called out to him, “My clothes are gone — I have given them all away in charity, and I cannot let myself be seen. Please hurry to the temple and send word; bid them bring me clothes at once.” In the end it was only when the temple sent someone with clothes and trousers that he climbed ashore. This old master was verily one who could “give up what is hard to give up.” Master Huiming gave away everything he had, and it became a treasured story of Hangzhou Buddhism.

The Elder Huiming was utterly of the common people, not given to luxury. The offerings that devotees ordinarily made him — fruit, sweets, cakes and pastries, and lengths of cloth — he never kept for himself, but at once sent attendants to the Ch’an hall, the recitation hall, and the hall for honored guests to be given away. When someone offered him a red packet, he would send the money to the storehouse to buy a meal for the community. He had a favorite catchphrase: “With all this entangling stuff lying about the room, I cannot sleep.” From this one may catch a glimpse of the old master’s freedom.

Though the Elder Huiming was a lecturing Dharma master and the foremost great abbot of a large monastery, he took no pride in his name and position, never swelled with self-importance, but was humble and approachable. His bearing was free and easy, like a spring breeze, warm and kindly; those of the pure community before him were seldom formal, and he delighted in mixing with them. Above all he felt closest to the ascetic monks of the menial offices, often chatting and joking with the hard-pressed vegetable cooks, gardeners, gatekeepers, and water keepers, and now and then helping plant vegetables, dig the ground, and carry slop — he would turn his hand to every kind of labor. In the seventeenth year of the Republic, when Mr. Chiang Kai-shek stepped down from power and went sightseeing at Lingyin Temple, drawn by the Elder’s spiritual bearing, he made a point of calling at the abbot’s quarters; he searched all about without finding him, until he went into the vegetable garden and there saw the Elder in a short shirt and tattered patched robe, holding a slop ladle and watering the vegetables. Mr. Chiang was charmed by his untrammeled manner, finding him frank and natural, never artificial, and so he stood in the garden conversing with him for a while.

The Elder Huiming’s bearing was always one of liberation. One year, Guiyuan Temple in Hubei invited him to lecture on the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment. When the appointed day came, all the temple’s officers and monks lined up in ranks at the mountain gate to receive him. They waited and waited for three days, yet still he did not come, and all wondered at it. On the fourth day, as the abbot was eating in the dining hall, he noticed in a corner seat — the seat of a lodging monk — a master who looked very much like the Elder Huiming. Looking closely, he saw that it was indeed the very Elder Master Huiming who had been invited to lecture. Overjoyed, when the meal was finished the abbot announced from his seat that everyone should not retire to their rooms but receive the Elder Master Huiming right there in the dining hall. All were bewildered! Where was the Master Huiming? Why receive him in the dining hall? It was the abbot who rose from his seat and went to the honored guest’s place and drew the Elder forth. At a glance all knew the truth: this sutra-lecturing master had long since arrived at the temple and was hiding in the guests’ quarters! In fact he had come five days earlier, presenting himself as a lodging monk; the guest master had not recognized him and had sent him to the guests’ quarters. The abbot at once kneeled and prostrated himself in apology, and bade the guest master beg the Elder’s forgiveness. The Elder said, “The guest master is not to blame for the breach of manners. I feared to disturb the assembly and would not presume, so I myself chose to lodge as a guest; I was content with a guest’s life.” Surely we see how liberated the Elder Master Huiming was!

The Elder Master Huiming had one odd temper: all his life he hated women who rouged and powdered themselves, and he hated nuns who decked themselves out smartly. When he met such a nun he would pout and could not help but say a few satirical words: “You dress yourself so prettily because you are pleased to be looked at by others, so in your next life you are sure to be a woman again.” Consequently the young nuns of the nunnery circles in Hangzhou, the moment they caught sight of the Elder, would hurry away in fear and dare not face him. Nor did he make exception for the wives and daughters of great officials and noblemen; he was wont to let fall a few cutting remarks, caring not whether the hearer could bear them. Judge Guan Jiongzhi of the International Mixed Court in Shanghai was one of the most renowned lay patrons in Shanghai Buddhist circles. His concubine, decked out in all her finery, came to call on the Elder and was given a merciless dose of the stick and the shout. She went home and wept for three whole days. In the end she took the Elder’s words to be a Dharma teaching spoken in compassion, and was moved to shame instead; she changed into plain clothes, put aside her powder and rouge, and went again to pay her respects to the Elder, asking for his instruction and taking refuge under him as his disciple. Such were the doings of the eminent monks of old — what of the eminent monks of today?

Master Huiming passed away in the winter month of the nineteenth year of the Republic, and his relics were enshrined beneath a pagoda raised at that temple. In the thirty-fourth year, when the War of Resistance was won, I disbanded the monk rescue corps and came eastward downriver from the provisional capital, resting a second time at Lingyin Temple; the monastery posted a notice inviting me as “hall master,” and I dwelt in the quarters beside the pagoda holding the Elder’s relics for three years.
